title: Interruptible mini-frames and tool-tokens: Mobile SDK PRD (draft)
content:
Summary
This PRD proposes a focused feature set for the Hosted API mobile SDK to support interruptible, progressively-delivered outputs ("mini-frames"), deterministic tool-call lifecycle management (tool-tokens and idempotency across partial responses), and a compact structured-output fallback format for unreliable networks. The aim is to make mobile integrations resilient to connectivity variability while keeping per-request latency predictable for small interactive flows (micro-interactions).

Problem statement
Mobile clients frequently operate on flaky networks, limited bandwidth, and strict battery/CPU constraints. Existing streaming semantics return long text deltas or large JSON payloads which are brittle on intermittent connectivity and hard for mobile apps to reconcile without complex client logic. Tool-calling from the model introduces additional complexity: tool calls may be initiated mid-stream, and clients need clear, idempotent semantics to execute, retry, or roll back tool invocations. Current Hosted API streaming patterns assume stable connections and server-side session continuity, which causes mobile apps to either: (a) buffer large partial outputs, (b) re-run logic on reconnect with inconsistent results, or (c) build fragile ad-hoc reconciliation layers.

Goals
- Deliver a lightweight streaming contract optimized for mobile: small, self-contained "mini-frame" units that convey partial text, structured fragments, and tool-call intent.
- Provide clear, server-generated tool-tokens and lifecycle events to make tool-call execution idempotent and resumable on reconnect.
- Define a compact structured-output fallback representation that can be embedded inline or requested in full on reconnect.
- Keep SDK ergonomics minimal: a concise public surface with default replay/merge heuristics so mobile app engineers can integrate quickly.
- Preserve observability and cost predictability: telemetry hooks for partial frames, tool execution outcomes, and reconnection events.

Non-goals
- Not addressing full desktop/long-running sessions or very large streaming transcripts (those remain covered by existing streaming PRDs).
- Not changing model-level generation algorithms—this is a contract/SDK and server-side orchestration design.

Key concepts and proposed contracts
1) Mini-frames
- A mini-frame is the atomic streaming unit delivered over the existing streaming protocol. Each frame is <= 2 KB compressed and contains: frame_id, seq (monotonic per session), payload_type (text_delta | struct_fragment | tool_signal | checkpoint), payload (string), timestamp, and optional resume_cursor.
- Clients apply frames in-order when possible. If a gap is detected (missing seq), client requests resume using resume_cursor. Frames are compact to favor many small updates rather than one large blob.

2) Checkpoints and resume_cursor
- Server emits periodic checkpoint frames with resume_cursor (opaque token). Resume_cursor encodes minimal state necessary to deterministically resume the streaming generation (model variant, prompt hash, up-to latest token id). On reconnect, client passes resume_cursor to get the next frames without re-generation or to receive a concise final structured artifact.

3) Tool-tokens and tool lifecycle events
- When model requests a tool call, server emits a tool_signal mini-frame describing: tool_id, intent_summary, tool_token (server-generated GUID), semantics (async | sync), and expected_cardinality (single | multi-part).
- Tool execution must be carried out by the client or a configured connector referencing tool_token. Tool_token ensures idempotency across retries and reconnections: server will accept the same tool_token and return consistent tool_response frames.
- Tool lifecycle events: tool_requested -> tool_sent -> tool_ack -> tool_result -> tool_committed/failed. Each mapped to mini-frames so the client can surface progress.

4) Structured-output fragment format
- Use a compact line-delimited JSONL fragment format for structured fragments inside frames (struct_fragment). Each fragment includes a schema_id and an incremental fragment_id. Clients can stitch fragments into a final artifact. If fragmentation is lost, client can request the final artifact via resume_cursor which will return a single compressed structured payload.

SDK ergonomics and example surface
- High-level API (pseudoflat):
  - startSession(options) -> sessionId
  - onFrame(sessionId, (frame) => handler) // frame is mini-frame object
  - resumeSession(sessionId, resumeCursor)
  - sendToolResponse(sessionId, toolToken, {result})
  - requestFinalStructured(sessionId)
- Default handlers: SDK provides a small default merger for text_delta frames that preserves word boundaries and a fragment reassembler for struct_fragment. App can override with onFrame.
- Mobile-specific optimizations: automatic low-power batching of frame processing when app in background, and a compact cache of resume_cursor per session persisted to secure local storage.

Observability and telemetry
- Emit token-level micro-metrics for: frames_received, frames_lost, resume_attempts, tool_requests, tool_retries, tool_latency, structured_fetches.
- Attach diagnostic tags to resume_cursor for server-side tracing (no PII).

Success metrics (90-day targets)
- 30% reduction in client-side reconcilation code across pilot apps.
- 50% fewer duplicated tool executions reported by pilot partners after enabling tool_tokens.
- Median time-to-first-mini-frame <= 120ms for small prompts under normal network.
- <2% increase in per-request token cost due to checkpointing overhead for typical micro-interactions.

Rollout plan
- Phase 0 (experimentation): internal SDK + server prototype, two pilot mobile apps, manual QA (6 weeks).
- Phase 1 (beta): public mobile SDK beta, opt-in feature flag, instrumented clients (8 weeks).
- Phase 2 (general availability): enable for all new mobile sessions by default with migration docs and deprecation timeline for legacy streaming paths (6–8 weeks after beta).

Risks and mitigations
- Resume_cursor opacity complexity: keep server tokens intentionally minimal; run load tests to ensure resume token replay doesn’t cause excessive re-generation.
- Tool_token security: tool_token must be short-lived and bound to sessionId; by default disallow sensitive tool execution in mobile autopilot mode.
- Increased telemetry cost: sample telemetry at 10% in beta, expand as needed.

Open questions
- Should resume_cursor be usable across devices (cross-device resume)? Pros: user convenience. Cons: increases server-side state complexity. Proposal: opt-in cross-device resume with explicit user tokens in a later phase.
- Default checkpoint frequency tradeoff: every 1s vs every N tokens. Need load testing to pick default; propose token-based adaptive checkpointing for initial experiment.

Next steps and owner actions (30 days)
- Engineering: prototype server-side resume_cursor and tool_token lifecycle (Marcus).
- SDK: ship mobile SDK alpha surface and default merger (Ravi).
- Product: run two pilot integrations and gather developer UX feedback (Sofia).
- Observability: instrument and create dashboard templates for the pilot metrics (Elena).

Appendix: short example flow
1) Client startSession -> server returns sessionId and first mini-frame (seq=1) with text_delta.
2) After few frames, server emits tool_signal with tool_token=abc123. Client shows an interstitial and sends tool execution result referencing abc123.
3) Network drops. Client persists resume_cursor X from last checkpoint.
4) On reconnect, client resumeSession(sessionId, resume_cursor=X). Server returns frames continuing from last committed token, then a struct_fragment final payload.

This document is intended to focus small, high-quality wins for mobile SDKs that reduce integration surface area and make tool-calling safe and reproducible in unreliable networks. Feedback welcome—particularly around resume semantics and tool execution security constraints.
